Author: brookieoz
Content:
It's important for a couple reasons:

1 - startup native vt device creates a current that shuts itself off once the bandgap starts up, causes the right side VBE to go up first. That creates a voltage delta in the amplifier

2 - the amplifier needs current otherwise it doesn't do anything, tail resistor with negative VTH means I don't need some kind of NMOS turnaround mirror. And the current is pretty stable because it's roughly always 0.5-0.6V

3 - amplifier input common mode voltage is quite low and to keep things simple I want NMOS input with PMOS mirror with PMOS CS output to reduce systematic mismatch from different Vds on input pair

4 - native VT devices typically match a lot better than full VT devices, important when it directly impacts bandgap voltage

Author: namibj
Content:
....a longer term project of mine I thought would use SiC JFETs who's gate source junction under forward bias is a really good temperature sensor about a channel thickness away from the channel itself was planned to use that to contain faults with coordinated emergency SCRAM's (it's a 10~30 kV to about 2~3 kV bidirectional converter aiming towards about a MW but a PoC would be built smaller power if just for parts costs; the dies are only rated 1200 or 1700 V!),

but they are all really high ohmic losses in the gate wiring presumably for avalanche proof behavior under cascode operation (if the drain leaks enough into the gate to turn the channel on before breakdown leakage through the reverse junction itself causes local damage, it's safe until the channel melts which takes literally several microseconds and thus easily several PWM cycles, so plenty of time to react and a brief transient is harmless),

 so I've pivoted to (ideally GaN V-JFETs if there are any smaller than 50$ a die with purchase limits of like one tray a month) likely epc-co GaN e-mode lateral MOSFET-substitutes which happily work at 50 MHz if you regeneratively/resonantly charge the gate and don't turn the channel on while there's drain voltage (output stored energy limits reasonable hard switch frequency to around 3 MHz typically for them) which sadly lack a thermal sense at the channel are not avalanche proof and who's gate is about 3x more finnicky than the SiC JFET (from formerly UnitedSiC).

After my SerDes efforts I hope to get to mod a microwave oven to use such a topology of likely 200/300 V epc-co devices to feed the magnetron with regulated DC of about 2kV from probably around 250~300 V nominal LiFePO4 battery backed "DC microgrid" that is also easily digestible by most computer PSUs and I think many induction stove tops and such.

I'm actually planning to use wafer.space to make an active digital pre-distortion driver for these power transistors that can talk with a central controller via (very short) fiber optics as it operates floating with severe switching transients (well, I expect around 20V/ns as "regular") and still has to coordinate for possible SCRAM.
It's switched capacitor technology using just enough inductance to not need to turn channels on with notable drain voltage remaining.
Oh, and poly-phase architecture allows it to neutralize ripple at the DC inputs and outputs greatly reducing the blocking demands put onto the EMI filters because if you have 1kW of e.g. 27 MHz "RF" power in the switched capacitors going down to micro watt levels of radiated leakage externally is... Hard.... If you try to maintain appliance-level 99% efficiency (if it was just a DC/DC transformer not a microwave with it's horrible magnetron).
